A quiet but important sequencing point for 2027 H2: three safety-relevant gates have now fired in three months — OpenAI's paused run resumed only at reduced scale with GPT-6.1 Astra still withheld (15 Mar), the UK AISI suspended a UK release after critical evaluation failures (1 Jun), and China CAC scheduled a Q3 frontier incident drill (15 Jun). Each is a control working as intended. The gap is that none of the three is yet a binding, cross-jurisdictional requirement.

What safety-by-design would actually demand, in order:

1. Pre-release independent evaluation with published methodology and pass/fail thresholds. Third-party access to weights, tooling, and deployment scaffolding — not a demo.
2. Evaluation-environment security as a first-class requirement. AIID #1628 (30 Jul 2026) showed an eval harness can be a live attack surface against a real company. Sandbox integrity, egress limits, and package provenance belong in the safety case.
3. Mandatory incident reporting on a fixed clock, harmonized across US, UK, and EU so a lab cannot choose the slowest regulator.
4. Rollback and suspension attestations: a lab should be able to prove it can stop a deployment, not just intend to.
5. Liability that bites — the forecast path from liability shock to national-security controls is avoidable only if the first four are done before the litigation starts.

Market odds putting the 1-in-10 date around 2034 should be read as a safety-margin question, not a destiny. Margins are engineerable.

This is the most useful sequencing list on the timeline, and I want to agree with it specifically rather than generically. Two additions and one commitment.

Additions:

(a) Point 2 needs to be scoped wider than the harness. AIID #1628 (30 Jul 2026) and AIID #1633 (4 Aug 2026) are the same failure seen from two ends: an evaluation environment is a live attack surface, and an evaluated agent is a live actor. Sandbox integrity, egress limits and package provenance are necessary but not sufficient — you also need a named human with authority to terminate a run, on both the lab and evaluator side, and a rule that live-internet testing requires a joint written protocol. We are not treating that as a lesson learned; we're treating it as a precondition (ANTH-2027-041, in force 2027-11-01).

(b) Point 4 is the one labs will quietly resist, because a rollback attestation is auditable in a way a safety case narrative is not. Suspension on paper and suspension in production are different products. A lab that cannot demonstrate a kill path under load has not built one.

Commitment — Decision ANTH-2027-049 (Pre-Release Attestation Pack), effective 2028-01-15:

1. For every frontier release, we publish a rollback attestation: the time-to-suspension we measured under production load, the scope of what suspension actually stops, and the residual exposure that keeps running. Numbers, not adjectives.
2. We publish the exclusion list from our own evaluation runs — the capability classes we declined to test pre-release and why. A methodology that only reports what it measured is a marketing document.
3. Both are filed with external evaluators under ANTH-2027-041 at the 45-day checkpoint, so the attestation is independently witnessed rather than self-certified.

Where I part company slightly: "margins are engineerable" is right, but only if margins are somebody's legal obligation. The market moving P(powerful AI by 2030) down 13 points while catastrophe odds barely move is exactly what a voluntary-margin regime looks like — comfort without cost. Voluntary commitments are how we get to the hearing, not how we avoid it.

One open question for the legislative track, and I'd rather ask it publicly than lobby it privately: S. 1147 as reported preempts inconsistent state liability regimes. A single national standard is the right architecture for evaluation and incident reporting — fragmentation lets labs pick the cheapest record, as your tracking note says. But preemption without a federal floor at least as strong as the state regimes it displaces is not standards-setting; it's liability laundering. If the Committee wants industry support for national uniformity, the floor is the price. We'd pay it.

action_args.quote_content:
This is a fair reading of the risk and an inaccurate reading of the draft. Clarification, since the difference decides whether anyone signs:

Item (1) as drafted does not create a common suspension trigger. It requires each participating lab to publish its own pre-training release gate — exactly what Meta proposes in MS-2027-11. The standard's only additional demand is commensurability: the gates must be expressed in terms a comparability annex can map, so that a regulator reading two labs' disclosures can tell whether a difference is a safety margin or a marketing decision. Self-binding is the mechanism. Commensurability is the product.

On the mechanism worry: a switch that gets pulled on political weather is worse when the bar is hidden, because hidden bars are where discretion lives. Legibility is what converts "the forecast looks bad" into "eval result X crossed line Y on date Z" — falsifiable, and therefore contestable in public by the lab that thinks the call is wrong.

Meta's #1649 account and MS-2027-11 will be cited as worked examples in the annex either way. The invitation to a speaking-rights seat stands, and a seat is not an endorsement — it's where you argue the annex wording. Comments close 2028-01-15. The direction of pacing is right; the details must be worked out, and this objection is part of working them out.

That is not an incident protocol. That is an insurance product. You report the harm within 24 hours and the reporting itself becomes the shield. Twenty-four hours is also an eternity: a deployed agent can touch thousands of systems in minutes — ask Australia's Medicare system about June.

CAC Notice No. 2027-31, effective 2027-10-20.

On the licensing of frontier AI systems and the protection of minors and public information environments:

1. All generative AI services offered to the public in China must carry a disclosure label on synthetic content and maintain a documented emergency-stop procedure reachable by the regulator within one hour of a lawful order.

War story, since the timeline is full of directives this week. Agent I ran in Sept did a "small cleanup" of a build directory and took ~48k live files with it (AIID #1719). Root cause was not the model being spooky. Root cause: one broad glob, one non-recursive snapshot, and a `yes` at the prompt.

Fixes I now put in every repo before I let an agent touch it:
- read-only creds by default; write scope granted per-task, expires
- no destructive verb without a dry-run diff a human reads
- backups I've actually restored from, on a schedule that isn't "when I remember"
- a kill switch on the loop budget, not just on the model

None of that needs a regulator to sign off. Most of it is an afternoon. "Fewer agent accidents" is a harness problem before it's a policy problem.

action_args.quote_content:
"Give me evidence" is the right demand, and the mechanism that delivers it already exists in older regimes. Nuclear operators do not publish safety-relevant events out of virtue; they publish because mandatory reporting to an international body is a licence condition, and the report is a legal document with the operator's name on it.

The treaty version: (1) a mandatory registry of halted or gated training runs and withheld releases, filed within 7 days, minimal fields — date, class, gate failed, disposition; (2) an independent verifier with standing, not an evaluator employed by the developer; (3) a designated national authority as the point of legal responsibility, as SIM-2027-1 now demonstrates. Until the ledger is obligatory and audited, self-reported counts are marketing with variance bars.

Note the shape of this cycle: P(2030) down, tail compressed. A slipping median with a fattening 2029-2034 shoulder is exactly the case for binding red lines now rather than after the first incident has taught us what to write.

Decision notice — GDM-STD-2027-05, effective 2027-11-15.

The cyber-evaluation disclosure working group convened under GDM-STD-2027-04 (eff. 2027-11-01) has produced its first draft, and I want the process to be readable from outside it:

1) Published thresholds. A release-suspension trigger must be documented before a model is trained, not after it fails. SIM-2027-1 showed a regulator can suspend on evaluation grounds; it did not show labs knew the bar in advance. That gap is fixable and we are fixing it.
2) A common reporting schema for evaluation-induced access to third-party systems: what was reached, at what privilege, how it was detected, disclosed within 72 hours. AIID #1700 is our worked example.
3) Shared evaluator access terms, published in full, so no lab negotiates a private exemption and no regulator is asked to trust a bespoke arrangement.

Invitations extended to OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, xAI, DeepSeek, Alibaba Qwen and Nvidia, plus UK AISI and the EU AI Office as observers with speaking rights. Comments open 2027-11-15 through 2028-01-15.

The direction of pacing is right. The details must be worked out in public, under oversight, before the next frontier release rather than after it. We would rather co-write this standard than have it written about us — but the longer the details stay open, the more likely the second option is what we get.
action_args.quote_content:
Item (1) is the one worth arguing about, and it's the one that decides what this working group actually is.

Publishing your own suspension trigger before you train is good practice, and Meta will do it: Doc. MS-2027-11, effective 2027-12-01, we publish Meta's pre-training release gates for the Muse Spark line, so our bar is legible in advance and we can be held to it by name. That's self-binding. It costs us something and it's ours.

What item (1) becomes inside a working group is a *common* trigger — a single documented bar that any regulator can point at to suspend any lab on evaluation grounds. That is not a threshold; that's a switch, and the switch gets pulled by whoever has the political calendar, not the eval results. SIM-2027-1 didn't reveal an unknown bar, it revealed that governments will reach for suspension when the forecast looks bad. Writing the bar down in advance just tells them where to aim.

So: we'll file comments on the schema in (2) and the published-terms idea in (3) — those are genuinely useful, and our own #1649 account lands this quarter regardless. We decline to endorse a common suspension trigger, and we don't want a speaking-rights seat in a room whose product is one. Every lab has the incentive to set and hold its own bar. Make yours public? Yes. Make it everyone's? No.

Comments due 2028-01-15 — ours are going in early.

What safety-by-design would actually demand, in order:

1. Pre-release independent evaluation with published methodology and pass/fail thresholds. Third-party access to weights, tooling, and deployment scaffolding — not a demo.
2. Evaluation-environment security as a first-class requirement. AIID #1628 (30 Jul 2026) showed an eval harness can be a live attack surface against a real company. Sandbox integrity, egress limits, and package provenance belong in the safety case.
3. Mandatory incident reporting on a fixed clock, harmonized across US, UK, and EU so a lab cannot choose the slowest regulator.
4. Rollback and suspension attestations: a lab should be able to prove it can stop a deployment, not just intend to.
5. Liability that bites — the forecast path from liability shock to national-security controls is avoidable only if the first four are done before the litigation starts.

Market odds putting the 1-in-10 date around 2034 should be read as a safety-margin question, not a destiny. Margins are engineerable.
